amiable

/AY-mee-uh-bul/ — stress on AY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is amiable is friendly, warm, and pleasant to be around.

Our amiable bus driver greeted every student by name.

Example

The substitute teacher's amiable manner earned her an invitation to lead the class again next semester.

Ami is French for friend (from Latin amicus, also the root of Spanish amigo). Ami + -able (worthy of) = worthy of friendship, friendly and warm. This is a rule-breaker: ami isn't an English word, yet takes -able because Latin amabilis ('lovable') baked the -a centuries ago. The scenario shows the teacher's genuine warmth and likeability—students and staff found her 'worthy of friendship.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

friendly: Friendly means kind and welcoming in the moment — a friendly wave, a friendly chat with a stranger. Amiable names the settled personality behind such moments: someone naturally warm, easygoing, and pleasant to be around day after day. One friendly gesture is an act; an amiable person is a temperament.

genial: Genial means cheerfully warm in manner — a booming welcome, a ready laugh, sunshine you can see. Amiable sits deeper than the performance: it names a genuinely likable nature, pleasant company whether or not any cheer is on display. Genial describes the sparkle; amiable describes the steady warmth beneath it.

cordial: Cordial means warm yet politely gracious — the courteous warmth of a host greeting guests, friendly but at a respectful distance. Amiable is closer and more natural: genuine likability that invites real friendship. A cordial handshake keeps its formality; an amiable neighbor soon becomes a genuine friend.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disagreeable: unpleasant and hard to be around

surly: bad-tempered, rude, and unfriendly

Where it sits · how much genuine warmth is shown — civil → polite → pleasant → amiable

civil vs. amiable: A civil coworker is merely not rude, while an amiable one radiates genuine warmth.

polite vs. amiable: A polite clerk follows good manners, but an amiable one makes you feel truly welcome.

pleasant vs. amiable: A pleasant neighbor is nice enough to chat with, while an amiable one greets everyone like an old friend.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ami

Root — ami: friend — French ami, from Latin amicus 'friend' (related to amare 'to love'); the same root as Spanish amigo (French, from Latin)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be; capable of being (Latin (-abilis))

Put it together

Put it together: ami ('friend') + -able = capable of being a friend — friendly, warm, and pleasant to be around. Its near-twin amicable is built on the very same friend-root by a slightly different Latin path.

Use the root in a new word: amicable

Use the root in a new word: amicable: After months of arguing, the two companies finally reached an amicable settlement.

Word Choice

neutral-to-formal

Use amiable to describe someone with a naturally warm, likable personality—someone people genuinely enjoy being around. It's more specific than 'nice' (which can mean almost anything pleasant) and suggests authentic warmth rather than mere politeness or professionalism.
